one_sentence_story: On sunny Arizona State campus walkways in 1975, Robert Cialdini and colleagues proved the 'Door-in-the-Face' effect — opening with a huge 2-year volunteer request (100% 'No!') and immediately conceding to a 2-hour zoo trip tripled 'Yes' rates from 16.7% to 50% because human reciprocity compels us to match someone else's concession with one of our own.
so_what_for_you: Protect yourself against artificial 'marked-down' sales concessions by evaluating Offer #2 strictly on its standalone value — and in ethical teamwork or fundraising, present an ambitious gold-standard option thoughtfully before offering a focused starter step.

jargon_map.plain: persuasion sequence where a large plausible request is turned down ('door slammed') and the same person immediately retreats to a smaller target request — tripling compliance
jargon_map.analogy: stepping back one pace in a dance so your partner instinctively steps forward one pace

jargon_map.plain: social fairness rule derived from the Norm of Reciprocity: if you soften your demand for me, I feel obliged to soften my refusal for you
jargon_map.analogy: meeting someone halfway when they compromise

jargon_map.plain: Cialdini's Experiment 2 proof that having a DIFFERENT person ask the small favor kills the boost because no concession was made by Person B
jargon_map.analogy: proving reciprocity — not just size contrast — drives the effect

jargon_map.plain: boundary rule that Request #1 must be believable rather than absurdly greedy, or else reciprocity turns into distrust
jargon_map.analogy: serious ambitious ask vs laughable joke price

jargon_map.plain: antidote against manipulative concessions: judging Offer #2 as if Offer #1 had never been spoken
jargon_map.analogy: wiping the crossed-out MSRP sticker off the tag
